headline: COP31 runs into a second day of overtime on a text that leaves out fossil fuels as African negotiators voice disappointment, while Wall Street slides into a correction on AI fears.

items.title: UN top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
items.summary: In a 9–6 decision on a case brought by The Gambia, the International Court of Justice found Myanmar responsible for genocide in northern Rakhine, the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the court. It ordered restitution, compensation and guarantees of non-repetition; Myanmar says its 2017 operation answered attacks on police posts.
items.why: A small West African country used international law to win a landmark case, a useful example for global-governance and policy studies.
items.videoQuery: ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling Rohingya Gambia

items.title: Ukraine and Russia trade blows over the Crimea bridge and record drone attacks
items.summary: Ukraine struck the Kerch Strait bridge to Crimea for a second day, collapsing part of the road section; Crimea's Russian-installed governor said two people died and traffic was halted. Russia said it downed a record 1,441 Ukrainian drones in a day, and Kyiv says its strikes answer Russian attacks on its infrastructure.

items.title: COP31 goes into a second day of overtime
items.summary: Summit president Murat Kurum said a text all parties could accept was ready for approval on Sunday, but the latest draft does not name fossil fuels, only alluding to the 2023 pledge to move away from them. It keeps the goal of electricity supplying 35% of final energy by 2035 and a call to speed up carbon capture, which some countries opposed.
items.why: The final wording shapes how ambitious countries' climate targets, and so demand for carbon credits, will be.
items.videoQuery: COP31 Antalya final day fossil fuels negotiations

items.title: African negotiators say COP31 outcomes fall short
items.summary: The African Group of Negotiators told the closing plenary that texts on climate education and long-term finance did not reflect Africa's positions, and urged the presidency to build consensus rather than impose an outcome. It also challenged an assessment of the $100bn finance goal for leaning on just two sources.
items.why: Ghanaians lead parts of Africa's climate diplomacy, so these positions are useful context for your Article 6 research.
items.videoQuery: African Group of Negotiators COP31 climate finance

items.title: Singapore signs its 14th Article 6 deal, with Zambia
items.summary: Singapore signed a binding implementation agreement with Zambia days after one with Kenya, making four African partners alongside Ghana and Rwanda. Both new deals send 5% of proceeds to adaptation in the host country and cancel 2% of authorised credits at first issuance.
items.why: Ghana already has a Singapore deal; these terms show what buyers expect and who Ghanaian sellers now compete with.
items.videoQuery: Singapore Article 6 carbon credit agreement Kenya Zambia

items.title: Electrification package becomes COP31's main concrete result
items.summary: The UN says more than 150 countries plus the EU, 37 cities and over 260 businesses back the COP31 electrification package, and host Türkiye says over $26bn in deals were agreed during the summit. Philanthropies also pledged more than $480m to cut methane and other super-pollutants.
items.why: Electrifying cooking and heat is close to what Carbon Clarity does with fish smoking.

items.title: Africa's own credit rating agency prepares its first scores
items.summary: The African Union's new Africa Credit Rating Agency, based in Mauritius, expects its first sovereign ratings by the end of March and is talking to 15 governments. Supporters say global agencies overstate African risk, while Moody's says its data show similar default rates for equal ratings, and critics worry about conflicts of interest because governments pay for ratings.
items.why: Ratings set borrowing costs for countries and for the climate projects they host.

items.title: €325m loan planned for water in Tamale, Damongo and Yendi
items.summary: Minister Haruna Iddrisu said a €325m loan agreement for water systems in three northern cities will go before Parliament next week. It still needs parliamentary approval, and no timeline was given.

items.title: Mahama defends the ban on chiefs in party politics
items.summary: Meeting the Oti Regional House of Chiefs, President Mahama backed the constitutional rule that bars chiefs from active party politics, citing a 2022 Supreme Court ruling. He said chiefs can still comment on policy and help local government through appointed seats.

items.title: Malawi's fuel shortage disrupts daily life
items.summary: Drivers in Malawi face rationing of about 20 litres a day and overnight queues, with black-market prices far above pump prices. The energy ministry blames shortages of money, foreign exchange and transport, and says it is working to restore supply; a civil-society group's planned protests were postponed by police.

items.title: Wall Street falls into a correction as the AI trade unravels
items.summary: On Friday the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% and the Nasdaq 5.3%, leaving the S&P 500 and Dow more than 10% below their records after the S&P's seventh straight daily fall. Nvidia sank about 14% and newly listed Anthropic lost about 9%, as traders also priced in a likely US rate rise in December.
items.why: A global risk-off mood can make investors more cautious about funding start-ups, including climate ventures.
items.videoQuery: stock market correction AI selloff Nvidia November 2026

items.title: US tightens rules on Chinese remote access to AI chips
items.summary: A new US Commerce Department rule requires licences for data centres anywhere that rent large amounts of advanced computing to China-headquartered firms, and for chip exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Some analysts welcomed it as closing a loophole, while others warned it could hurt countries such as Malaysia.
items.videoQuery: US rule remote access AI chips China data centers

items.title: IEA: sub-Saharan Africa set to nearly double renewable capacity
items.summary: The IEA's Renewables 2026 report expects the region to add over 120 GW of renewables between 2026 and 2031, more than 80% of it solar, with about two-thirds of new solar coming from homes, businesses and off-grid systems. It trimmed its utility-scale forecast because of financing and grid limits.
items.why: Distributed solar for small businesses is a growing market Carbon Clarity's processors could tap.

items.title: Moon dust turned into LEGO-like bricks
items.summary: University of Arkansas researchers used lasers to fuse simulated lunar soil into interlocking bricks with no binder, a possible way to build on the Moon from local material. The bricks are still small, porous and not yet strong enough to bear loads.

items.title: Precise light measurements for a key crystal could speed up internet hardware
items.summary: A KAIST-led team with Caltech measured how barium titanate bends and absorbs light across a very wide range of wavelengths, filling a long-standing data gap. The results, in ACS Photonics, could help design faster optical communication devices.

items.title: NASA fires a Moon-rocket engine for a full 200 seconds
items.summary: A developmental RS-25 engine ran for its full planned duration at Stennis Space Center, giving data to improve flight engines for the Space Launch System. The work supports the Artemis IV mission planned for 2028.
items.videoQuery: NASA RS-25 engine test Stennis November 2026

good.title: Zambia locks in $60m for a 50 MW solar plant
good.summary: Zambia signed an investment protection deal with a Malaysian-backed company for a 50 MW solar farm in Chilanga that has reached financial close, with about 300 construction jobs expected.

good.title: Ghana's Black Challenge beat the USA at the Amputee World Cup
good.summary: Ghana's amputee football team beat the USA 3-1 in Mexico to reach the World Cup quarter-finals, and the Ghana News Agency reports they went on to reach the semi-finals.

good.title: Clean-water filters for 1.8 million Rwandans get carbon-credit backing
good.summary: Singapore authorised its first project under its Rwanda carbon deal: 300,000 ceramic water filters expected to benefit about 1.8 million people and avoid around 780,000 tonnes of CO2 by 2030.
good.why: A close model for how a household-device project like clean ovens can earn Article 6 credits.

good.title: Over $480m pledged to cut methane
good.summary: Philanthropic funders at COP31 pledged more than $480m to reduce methane and other short-lived super-pollutants, among the fastest ways to slow warming.

good.title: Africa's renewables set to nearly double by 2031
good.summary: The IEA expects sub-Saharan Africa to add more than 120 GW of renewable power in six years, led by rooftop, business and off-grid solar.

quiz.q: By what vote did the International Court of Justice find Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya?
quiz.why: The court ruled 9-6 in the case brought by The Gambia.

quiz.q: Singapore's new Article 6 agreement with Zambia is its bilateral deal number…
quiz.why: Zambia was the 14th, after Kenya (13th); Ghana and Rwanda are its other African partners.

quiz.q: Where is the African Union's new Africa Credit Rating Agency based?
quiz.why: AfCRA is headquartered in Port Louis and expects first ratings by end of March.

future.title: Clean cooking financed by carbon credits
future.why: New government policies across Africa have helped secure about $900 million in new clean-cooking finance, with carbon credits as the main engine. The catch: it only lasts if buyers trust the credits.
future.fit: This is Carbon Clarity's core. The winners will be projects with measured, audit-ready data.
future.step: This month: map which Gold Standard metered-method requirements your pilot data already meets.

future.title: Digital MRV and high-integrity credit data
future.why: Credit buyers increasingly pay only for credits they can verify. Sensor-based monitoring and clean data trails are becoming the difference between credits that sell and credits that don't.
future.fit: Your Data Vault idea could become a service for other cookstove and agriculture projects in Ghana.
future.step: Write a one-page description of the Data Vault as a service: who pays, what it proves.

future.title: Clean heat for small industries
future.why: RMI lists clean industrial heat among Africa's six emerging climate-tech opportunities. Fish smoking is exactly this: small-scale process heat.
future.fit: Improved ovens for fish processors are a clean-heat business with income for women, not just a stove programme.
future.step: Estimate the market: how many processors in Greater Accra and coastal Ghana, and how much wood they burn.

future.title: Carbon removal from biomass: biochar
future.why: RMI also highlights carbon dioxide removal that uses Africa's biomass and soils, a market where removal credits sell for far more than avoidance credits.
future.fit: Waste biomass from smoking (husks, offcuts) could be turned into biochar: a second revenue stream.
future.step: Read one biochar removal methodology and list what you'd need to measure.

future.title: Energy-led climate tech is where African investment goes
future.why: Africa's climate-tech startups raised $6.35bn from 2016 to 2025, now the continent's biggest venture sector, with energy taking about 65% of the money.
future.fit: Pitch Carbon Clarity as energy plus livelihoods: efficient heat, solar drying or cold storage for fish.
future.step: Add one slide to your pitch: 'Why energy investors should care about fish smoking'.

future.title: Article 6 advisory for Ghanaian projects
future.why: Ghana is one of the first countries trading credits between governments under Article 6. Developers need people who understand authorisation, corresponding adjustments and the Carbon Market Office process.
future.fit: Your Ghana carbon market research makes you one of those people: it can become consulting work or a job.
future.step: Turn your Step 3 agreement table into a two-page brief you can share on LinkedIn.
